content.thinking:
I'm mapping out the directory structure for the mesh generator module, starting with the schema definitions covering palettes, rifle, crate, sword, and kit specs along with validation types.

Beyond that, I'm planning the remaining modules: template registry, catalog matching, routing, cost estimation, scratch script scanning, GLB validation, budget checks, output manifest building, the Blender runner and worker loop, model-facing contracts, feature flags, and the Blender-side Python scripts for harness, geometry assembly, scratch guarding, and the rifle/crate/sword templates themselves.

For testing, I'm sketching a unit test file plus a separate Blender-dependent test that only runs on node-2 when the Blender environment variable is set, skipping gracefully otherwise. There's also a Python test script run inside Blender itself to validate each template against fixtures, and a flights script for real end-to-end checks.

I need to figure out how the runner accesses the Python template files — reading them from the repo directory server-side, then content-hashing them to track kit version and record provenance via a sha256 harness signature. For execution on node-2, the plan is to send a tar stream over stdin containing the input files and sandbox script, then receive a base64-encoded tar of outputs (glb files and PNG renders) back over stdout.

For the sandbox script itself, I'm working out where it lives on node-2 — the Blender build is already downloaded at a known tmp path, so the sandbox script needs to point to that binary rather than re-downloading. I should verify the tarball's sha256 against a hash file once and log that verification in the flight record rather than re-checking every run.

I'm shipping the launcher script inside each job tarball rather than installing it separately, so the remote command just extracts the archive into the job directory, runs the launcher with the job path, Blender binary, and timeout, then tars up the work output and base64-encodes it for transfer before cleaning up the job directory.

Output needs to stay separate from sandbox logs though, so I'll have the launcher redirect Blender's stdout to a log file inside work, write harness stats to a JSON file, and capture the exit code into a meta directory outside work since work is untrusted and writable by the sandboxed user. I also need to make sure the work and home directories are owned by the unprivileged "nobody" user the sandbox runs as.

I should cap output size with a du check after the run, only accept expected filenames, and treat symlinks carefully since tar won't dereference them by default — I'll write a minimal ustar parser on the receiving side that only extracts regular files matching the allowed names. Cleanup of the job directory also needs the path validated against a strict id regex before any recursive delete.

For locking, the sandbox script acquires a flock on a dedicated lock file, held only for the duration of the Blender render, with a bounded wait time; the overall SSH timeout needs to account for lock wait plus render time plus margin, and jobs that exceed their timeout get swept and discarded. Rendering itself uses Cycles at low sample count across three views for a quick preview, controlled by a render option that can be turned off entirely.

After building, if triangle count exceeds budget and decimation is allowed, the harness applies a collapse-based decimate per object by ratio, though this can break manifoldness which later checks would catch — I want to deliberately test this path with a tiny triangle budget on a flight to confirm it works. For UV, I'm using smart_project per object as a proof of concept, checking for layer presence and coverage range but not overlaps, which I'll just flag as unchecked.

Now I'm defining per-object checks (triangles, non-manifold edges, shells, degenerate faces, loose verts, material count, UV presence, bbox) and global checks (total triangles, object/material counts, bbox, glb size, re-import triangle count), then sketching the TypeScript MeshBudget type with optional per-category overrides for triangle and bbox limits, noting that LODs aren't actually generated yet so I'll surface that as a documented warning.

I'm now working through severity handling: should an "error" issue fail the queue job outright with nothing saved, or should the worker still store the record (including renders) so a model can iterate and fix it next round? I'm leaning toward completing the job with output marked as rejected rather than losing the record entirely.

For rung 0 catalog matches there's no worker job at all — the router just returns candidates and the build service pulls the catalog asset directly, with the worker rejecting any rung 0 requests as bad_request. For accounting, record.tokens should carry rung, the request's estimate, actual usage from the build service, and rounds, while record.compute captures wallMs, blenderMs, and lockWaitMs — the worker never invents these numbers itself. Now I need to work out the router's template registry with keyword matching per template type, like rifle-related terms versus crate-related terms.

I'm sketching the sword keyword set, then thinking about whether templates can be toggled per game via an availability input. I'm also laying out the broader category taxonomy — ranged/melee weapons, containers, props, vehicles, characters, creatures, furniture, other — and deciding organic subjects (people, animals, plants) get routed to character/creature categories or flagged by keyword, since rung 3 handles organic poorly. The plan is the router refuses character/creature requests outright with an "unsupported" reason since there's no rigging support, but lets plain organic props like trees or rocks through to rung 3.

Characters and creatures get refused outright, while other objects route to rung 2 if they're hard-surface-ish or rung 3 otherwise — rung 2 fits most generic hard-surface props when no template matches and the prompt lacks organic/curvy keywords like statue, cloth, or plush, with organic ones falling to rung 3 deterministically. I'm also designing a cost estimation function that returns rounds, token counts, and dollar totals before running a job, pulling prices from host settings keys with no invented defaults — if unconfigured, dollars stays null with a "price not configured" note.

Now I'm working out token estimates per rung per round: rung 0 is a single quick query call; rung 1 uses cached cards plus image/stats input with measured ranges around 5.2-8k tokens; rung 2 assumes roughly 3 rounds with kit cards and parts-list output, marked as "assumed" since it's unmeasured; and rung 3 scales further with larger cached preludes, bigger outputs, and more rounds.

I'm noting the max caps per rung for rounds and output tokens, and clarifying that each build job corresponds to one round in the service loop — submit, render, adjust. I'm also sketching the contract's `mesh_route` tool, which takes a prompt/category/game and returns a route decision with an estimate from the router service.

I'm now filling in the remaining build tools — `mesh_build_template`, `mesh_build_kit`, and the premium `mesh_build_script` — along with the shared `MeshToolResult` response shape and the system card text, and checking whether zod v4's `toJSONSchema` is available for exporting tool schemas.

I'm settling on env flags like `CYRUS_MESHGEN` and `CYRUS_MESHGEN_SCRATCH` to gate the worker and submit paths, keeping consistent with the existing env-flag pattern, and confirming the host seam only imports lib/cyrus, node builtins, and zod.

Now I'm designing the Python geometry generator, generalizing slot sets per template type — rifle, crate, sword — each with their own part names like body/furniture/barrel or hull/frame/panel.

I'm refactoring to pass slots and defaults into a generic `make_materials` and `Part` class, replacing the global SIDX with an instance attribute, and defining the standard template module interface: each tpl file exposes `TEMPLATE_ID`, `VERSION`, `SLOTS`, `DEFAULT_PAL`, `PART_NAMES`, and a `build(spec)` function that returns the generated objects.

On the TS side, TemplateDef registers the Zod schema, keywords, card, and Python module name, with validation happening both in TS and defensively via ValueError in Python. For the harness, I'm designing the request format (rung, template, spec/kit/scratch file, budget, render settings, name) and the build steps: clearing the scene, running the module, verifying mesh outputs, applying UV smart projection, and cleaning up non-mesh objects for scratch builds before gathering stats.

Next comes decimation if needed, re-stats, GLB export with re-import verification, rendering, and writing stats.json, all wrapped in try/except so failures produce a structured error object -- plus I need to handle Blender's exit code behavior since exceptions don't naturally propagate without the `--python-exit-code` flag. For scratch scripts, I'm also thinking through sandboxing: an AST guard before execution, then providing a restricted namespace with Part, make_materials, and a mesh_objects list so the script can safely build geometry.

I'm designing the `build(K)` interface where K exposes part creation, named slots, and a finish step that converts parts into actual objects, while also allowing restricted bpy/bmesh access for advanced geometry but blocking dangerous operators like file export/import, rendering, scripting, and preferences access.

Expanding the denylist...

Since the harness already applies modifiers on export, I realize I can deny `bpy.ops` entirely since it's stronger and simpler—scripts can rely on bmesh plus bpy.data instead. But I need to be careful since `bmesh.ops` is distinct from `bpy.ops` and shouldn't be blocked by the same attribute name check, so the AST inspection needs to distinguish module paths rather than just the bare attribute name.

I'm settling on a concrete policy: allow only specific imports like math, random, bmesh, mathutils, and bpy, while blacklisting dangerous builtins such as eval, exec, compile, open, __import__, globals, locals, getattr, and setattr, plus denying any attribute access starting with an underscore and blocking specific risky bpy attributes.

I'm also deciding to detect and deny bare `bpy` references used for aliasing, rather than only as attribute bases, and to implement both a Python AST-based gate as the authoritative pre-run check inside the sandbox and a lighter TypeScript token/regex-based scan for pre-submit validation, with both explicitly documented as convenience checks rather than true security boundaries.

Now I'm defining the restricted builtins dictionary, limiting execution to safe functions like len, range, sorted, isinstance, and a guarded `__import__` that only permits allowlisted modules, since bpy itself exposes dangerous escape hatches like opening URLs. I'm also starting to sketch the "Rung 2" kit spec for generating objects from palettes, slots, and parts with configurable shapes and groupings.

Writing shape variant logic...

I'm capping complexity with limits on groups, dimensions, and bounding box size, keeping everything JSON-only and deterministic. I'm now sketching out the crate template spec with style/lid/corner/panel/handle/latch options and a wooden variant using slats with metal bands, then starting on the sword template spec for blade style options.

For the blade itself I'm planning to build it as a diamond cross-section loft along its length, manually constructing the mesh station by station with varying half-width and centerline offset.

Adding more edge vertices...

For the rifle template, I plan to reuse the pistol rifle and parts modules largely as-is. I'm noting export orientation conventions per template — rifle muzzle along +X, sword blade along +Z with grip at origin, crate base at z=0 — and that views will be configured per template module for rendering.

Now I'm sketching the TS GLB validator: it checks the file header magic and version, validates JSON and binary chunk headers, confirms asset version, checks primitive modes and accessor counts against triangle counts, verifies buffer views stay within buffer bounds, flags any external URIs in buffers or images as invalid for GLB format, and counts materials and nodes.

I also want to require POSITION accessors to include min/max for bounding box computation, computing a naive bbox that ignores node transforms since parts are built in world coordinates already, and tallying triangle counts across all mesh instances referenced by nodes. Then I'm writing a basic ustar tar parser in TS that extracts filename, size, and type flag fields to only accept regular files matching an allowlist of output naming patterns.

Now I'm sketching the Node-2 Blender runner interface: a factory that wires up remote execution, root/blenderDir paths, and Python scripts, exposing a `run` method that takes a job request and returns a structured result with status, exit code, parsed result.json, extracted files (glb, renders, sheet), log tail, and timing metadata.

I'm also drafting the privileged launcher script that runs outside the sandbox on node-2 -- it validates the job directory path, checks Blender's binary exists, sets up work/home/meta directories with correct ownership and permissions, then starts timing the execution.

The script acquires a flock to serialize mesh generation jobs, records lock wait time, and launches Blender via systemd-run with a dedicated unit and resource slice, capturing stdout/stderr to a log file and recording the final exit code and timing in the job's meta directory.

I'm now worrying that the Blender log could grow unbounded if the user script runs a print loop, since RuntimeMax only bounds wall-clock time, not disk usage -- I should cap the log size, maybe with `head -c` or a periodic truncate, while being careful about exit-code preservation with pipefail and PIPESTATUS.

I also need to think about the work directory itself: a sandboxed user could write huge files there, and since there's no built-in disk quota property in systemd, I'm considering mounting a size-limited tmpfs for the work directory instead.

That approach means the output data would vanish once the unit stops, so I'd need root to mount a capped tmpfs before running and unmount it after collecting results — adding a cleanup trap to avoid leftover mounts if something crashes, while keeping in mind tmpfs memory usage still counts against the unit's memory cgroup limit.

I'm sketching the collection step: after the sandboxed run finishes, tar up the work and meta directories into an output archive, unmount the tmpfs, then have the outer command base64-encode and emit that archive before cleaning up the whole scratch directory.

For sandbox limits I'm adding a per-file size cap and disabling core dumps, then mirroring the earlier PoC sandbox properties but adjusting the bind paths for the new input/work/home layout -- trying to figure out whether HOME should live inside the tmpfs work dir or just point somewhere simple like /tmp under PrivateTmp, since Blender may want a writable config directory.

PrivateTmp risks filling the node's root disk, so I'm switching to TemporaryFileSystem for /tmp with a size cap and sticky mode, and figuring out whether Blender can safely create its config directory under a HOME pointing into that tmpfs.

Since TemporaryFileSystem content is charged to the unit's memory limit, this should stay within bounds, and ordering-wise the bind mounts for /tank get applied after the tmpfs hides it, matching how the PoC worked. Blender runs headless without GPU/X needs, so I'm confirming the build path and version under /tank/nxeon-build/tmp/blender-poc.

For the flights script, I'm running meshgen-flights.ts via devhost run on node-2 using a local spawned-bash Remote, then pulling back renders and JSON results with devhost pull. Since devhost run executes as a nested systemd service with dbus access, the worker loop can enqueue jobs through the memory job queue and let each Blender invocation acquire its own build lock rather than locking at the devhost run level.

Within that run-capped unit, mounting a tmpfs would happen in the host mount namespace since there's no sandboxing or private mounts configured, which seems fine and avoids relying on filesize/count limits to control disk usage from a script writing many large files. I'm also noting that the shared build tmp directory is world-writable with the sticky bit set.

For the node-2 template test, I need to run it through devhost directly rather than devhost test, since the latter would deadlock by trying to take a lock the runner already holds. There's also a separate Python-based test script that runs inside the Blender sandbox to build each template.

I'm thinking a "selftest" harness mode would be useful: iterate over all template variant combinations, build each one, check nonmanifold counts, and write results to a JSON file without rendering or exporting, giving coverage of untested variants like drum and rail_quad. The per-object budget checks happen in the harness and get verified against budgets in the TS test. For decimation, I need to figure out whether the harness itself applies it via Blender's modifier API or handles it some other way.

I should also set the active context properly if using ops-based decimation, which should be fine in Blender 5.x. Then I want to double-check the Zod version and see how other Cyrus modules export their JSON schemas.

#!/bin/bash
# sbx-meshgen.sh -- run ONE meshgen job's Blender inside the node-2 sandbox (recipe from the 2026-10-10 PoC, sbx.sh).
# Runs as root ON node-2, outside the sandbox. Shipped inside each job's tar by lib/cyrus/meshgen/runner.ts.
#   sbx-meshgen.sh JOBDIR BLENDER_DIR MAX_SEC LOCK_WAIT_SEC
# JOBDIR/in   = harness + modules + request.json (+ scratch.py), read-only inside the sandbox
# JOBDIR/work = size-capped tmpfs owned by nobody, the only writable path inside the sandbox
# Writes JOBDIR/out.tar (work/ regular files + meta/) for the caller to fetch, then unmounts the tmpfs.
# Exit codes in meta/exit: blender's own, 75 = build lock busy, 124 = killed at RuntimeMaxSec.
set -uo pipefail
J="$1"; B="$2"; MAX="$3"; WAIT="$4"
ROOT=/tank/nxeon-build/tmp/meshgen/jobs
case "$J" in "$ROOT"/mg-*) ;; *) echo "bad job dir" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
case "$(basename "$J")" in *[!a-z0-9-]*) echo "bad job id" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
case "$MAX$WAIT" in *[!0-9]*) echo "bad limits" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
[ "$(hostname)" = nxeon-fsn1 ] || { echo "must run on node-2" >&2; exit 2; }
[ -x "$B/blender" ] || { echo "no blender at $B" >&2; exit 2; }
mkdir -p "$J/work" "$J/meta"
chmod 755 "$J" "$J/in"; chmod 644 "$J/in"/*
mount -t tmpfs -o size=512m,mode=0755,uid=65534,gid=65534,nosuid,nodev,noexec cyrus-meshgen "$J/work" || { echo 70 > "$J/meta/exit"; exit 0; }
cleanup() {
  # copy only regular files (never symlinks/devices the sandbox may have made), capped at 64 MB in total
  ( cd "$J" && find work -maxdepth 1 -type f -size -48M -printf '%P\n' | head -40 | sed 's|^|work/|' > meta/files.txt
    tar --no-recursion -cf out.tar -T meta/files.txt meta/exit meta/log.txt meta/lock_wait_ms meta/wall_ms 2>/dev/null
    [ "$(stat -c %s out.tar 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" -le 67108864 ] || : > out.tar )
  umount "$J/work" 2>/dev/null || umount -l "$J/work" 2>/dev/null || true
}
trap cleanup EXIT
: > "$J/meta/log.txt"; echo 0 > "$J/meta/lock_wait_ms"; echo 0 > "$J/meta/wall_ms"
t0=$(date +%s%3N)
exec 7>>/run/lock/nxeon-build.lock
if ! flock -w "$WAIT" 7; then echo 75 > "$J/meta/exit"; exit 0; fi
t1=$(date +%s%3N); echo $((t1 - t0)) > "$J/meta/lock_wait_ms"
UNIT="cyrus-meshgen-$(basename "$J")"
systemd-run --quiet --pipe --wait --collect --unit="$UNIT" --slice=nxeon-build-agents.slice \
  -p Nice=10 -p IOSchedulingClass=best-effort -p IOSchedulingPriority=7 -p OOMScoreAdjust=1000 \
  -p RuntimeMaxSec="$MAX" -p KillMode=control-group -p TimeoutStopSec=5 \
  -p User=nobody -p Group=nogroup \
  -p MemoryMax=4G -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p CPUQuota=400% -p TasksMax=256 -p LimitCORE=0 -p LimitFSIZE=268435456 \
  -p PrivateNetwork=yes -p ProtectSystem=strict -p ProtectHome=tmpfs \
  -p TemporaryFileSystem=/tmp:size=256M,mode=1777 \
  -p TemporaryFileSystem=/opt:ro -p TemporaryFileSystem=/tank:ro -p TemporaryFileSystem=/mnt:ro -p TemporaryFileSystem=/srv:ro -p TemporaryFileSystem=/var/lib:ro \
  -p TemporaryFileSystem=/etc/pve:ro -p TemporaryFileSystem=/etc/nxeon-build:ro \
  -p BindReadOnlyPaths="$B" -p BindReadOnlyPaths="$J/in" -p BindPaths="$J/work" \
  -p ProtectKernelTunables=yes -p ProtectKernelModules=yes -p ProtectKernelLogs=yes -p ProtectControlGroups=yes -p ProtectClock=yes \
  -p NoNewPrivileges=yes -p CapabilityBoundingSet= -p RestrictNamespaces=yes -p LockPersonality=yes -p RestrictSUIDSGID=yes \
  -p WorkingDirectory="$J/work" \
  -E HOME=/tmp -E TMPDIR=/tmp -E LANG=C.UTF-8 -E PATH=/usr/bin:/bin \
  "$B/blender" --background --factory-startup --python-exit-code 3 --python "$J/in/mg_harness.py" -- "$J/in/request.json" \
  </dev/null 2>&1 | head -c 262144 > "$J/meta/log.txt"
rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
t2=$(date +%s%3N); echo $((t2 - t1)) > "$J/meta/wall_ms"
# systemd-run reports a RuntimeMaxSec kill as a failed unit; record it as 124 so the caller can say "timeout"
if [ "$rc" -ne 0 ] && [ $((t2 - t1)) -ge $((MAX * 1000)) ]; then rc=124; fi
echo "$rc" > "$J/meta/exit"
flock -u 7
exit 0

content.thinking:
The noexec mount shouldn't matter since Blender doesn't need to execute anything from that work directory, and the cleanup trap still fires correctly even on the early exit path when flock fails. For listing output files, I'm using find with maxdepth and a size filter to get paths relative to the work directory, then prefixing them appropriately — and since find doesn't follow symlinks by default, type-file filtering naturally excludes them.

Since the sandbox unit is fully stopped before tar reads the file list, there's no TOCTOU race between enumeration and archiving, and tar's default non-dereferencing behavior keeps things safe. Permissions on the job directories and tmpfs-mounted paths all trace back to root's default umask, so traversal should work fine throughout the chain.

content.thinking:
The crate looks good, but the sword's camera framing is off — it's tall and thin, so the vertical frame is cropping it at top and bottom, and I'd also mixed up the azimuth so the "broadside" view was actually showing the edge-on thin profile instead. I need to fix the camera distance calculation and correct which azimuth angle gives the broadside view.

For a sword rendered full-height in a landscape frame, maybe I should just add a portrait render resolution override for that template since contact sheets just need matching heights. And I should generalize the distance formula using the bounding sphere radius so the camera distance accounts for the object's actual proportions rather than a fixed multiplier.

I'll keep the current distance factor since crates frame well with it, but add a fit-distance check based on vertical and horizontal extents to make sure larger objects aren't cropped. The sword's blade looks a bit pale and flat in this broadside lighting, but that's acceptable for a template since models can adjust the palette themselves.

Now I'm accounting for Blender's default camera sensor behavior—36mm sensor with AUTO fit, where the larger image dimension determines whether horizontal or vertical framing applies.

All pass now, so I move on to the real Blender test file for node-2 and the flights script, planning to run flights via devhost run instead of --lock. I confirm that nested systemd-run inside the devhost unit should work since it's root and the hostname check still passes, and mount isn't namespace-restricted in a service context. Then I start looking at the flight script at scripts/cyrus/meshgen-flights.ts.

The script takes a --out directory argument relative to the node-2 worktree, uses a local transport runner since it executes on node-2 directly, and verifies the Blender tarball against its sha256 file while recording the Blender version. It queues flights in-memory, routes each one with availability scratch enabled to record the routing decision, submits or directly enqueues, runs the worker loop for one job, captures timing, writes glb/render outputs, and validates them with the Khronos gltf-validator to parse errors and warnings. I also need to run the selftest directly through the runner since the worker path doesn't support it, then write everything to a JSON summary before pulling the output directory back via devhost.

No migration, enum or table. check in TS), `checks.ts` (`HarnessResultZ`, `checkMesh`: budget, per-object manifold/UV/degenerate/loose, extent per category,
glb re-import and triangle cross-checks, LOD warning), `scan.ts` (rung 3 static scan), `output.ts` (manifest + `MeshgenRecord`),
`runner.ts` (server only), `worker.ts` (server only), `contract.ts` (model-facing tools, types only), `blender/` (Python data files + `sbx-meshgen.sh`).

(omitted = old behaviour) so a meshgen worker never claims another linux-cpu job.

enqueues `{type: "meshgen", workerClass: "linux-cpu", inputs: [requestKey]}` (timeouts 8 min template/kit, 12 min scratch).
`runMeshgenWorker` (pull loop: sweep, claim, process, one job at a time) -> `processMeshgenJob`: re-validates, builds the harness
request, calls the injected `BlenderRunner`, validates `result.json`, parses the glb, runs the checks. **Fail closed:** any error issue =
verdict `rejected`, no glb and no manifest stored (renders are stored for the next model round). Job outputs: `outputs[0]` is ALWAYS the
record (`kind: cyrus-meshgen-record`: verdict, issues, stats, decimation, object keys, tokens {estimate, usage}, compute {wall, lock wait,
Blender s, exit}, engine {Blender version, harness version, sha256 of the shipped code, runner}). A queue job "done" means the worker
finished, read `record.verdict`. Busy build lock / transport failure -> `not_run`, job `failed` (resubmit). Timeout/crash -> `rejected`.
A job the sweep expired meanwhile is not completed (the record stays in the store).

optional `scratch.py`) to `/tank/nxeon-build/tmp/meshgen/jobs/mg-<id>-<rand>/in`, runs `sbx-meshgen.sh` there as root: mounts a 512 MB
tmpfs (uid nobody, noexec) as the work dir, takes `/run/lock/nxeon-build.lock` (wait <= 600 s, exit 75 = busy), runs Blender 5.2.2 LTS
(`/tank/nxeon-build/tmp/blender-poc/blender-5.2.2-linux-x64`, tarball sha256 `84098912...a168` = the published file, re-checked in the
flights) via `systemd-run` in `nxeon-build-agents.slice`: User=nobody, PrivateNetwork, ProtectSystem=strict, /opt /tank /mnt /srv
/var/lib /etc/pve /etc/nxeon-build hidden, 256 MB tmpfs /tmp, MemoryMax 4G no swap, CPUQuota 400%, TasksMax 256, LimitFSIZE 256 MB,
no capabilities, NoNewPrivileges, RuntimeMaxSec. Only regular files (<48 MB each, <=40, <=64 MB total) are copied back, base64 over
stdout; the job dir is deleted. **A systemd unit is not a VM: a kernel escape is untested. Production rung 3 must also run on an
isolated worker (microVM/gVisor).**

sandbox is the boundary.

-> export glb -> Cycles CPU contact sheet (3 views, 32 spp, FOV-aware framing, portrait for tall templates) -> re-import the glb -> always
writes `result.json` with a structured `{stage, type, message}` error on failure. `rung: "selftest"` builds every template's `SELFTEST`
matrix (every enum value) plus negative cases.

**Adding a template** (rung 1): (1) write `blender/tpl_<id>.py` with `TEMPLATE_ID`, `VERSION`, `SLOTS`, `DEFAULT_PAL`, `VIEWS`
(optional `RENDER_RES`), `SELFTEST` (cover every enum value) and `build(spec) -> [objects]` using `mg_geo.Part` (`box`, `cyl`,
`sphere`, `tube`, `rod`, `prism`, `loft`; every primitive a closed shell) + `make_materials` + `finish`; raise `ValueError` naming the
allowed values on a bad enum; (2) add the module to `MODULES['template']` in `mg_harness.py`; (3) add a strict Zod schema to `spec.ts`
(palette over the same slots) and a `TemplateDef` in `templates.ts` (module, deps, categories, keywords, excludes, a <= 1.2k-char card,
an example, `tokenBasis: "assumed"` until measured); (4) run `test/cyrus-meshgen.test.ts` (checks id/version/slots match and that every
enum value appears in the Python) and the real suite on node-2; (5) bump `VERSION` on any change that alters geometry.

**Model-facing contract** (`contract.ts`, not wired): the service routes, shows the estimate, then gives the model ONE forced tool
(`mesh_template` with that template's strict schema, `mesh_kit`, or `mesh_script`), system prompt = rules + the card (cacheable),
`max_tokens` = the rung's `maxOutputPerRound`; each build returns `toolResultFor(record)` (errors first, <= 12 issues, stats vs budget,
rounds left, next = revise/stop/retry_later) plus the contact sheet as an image; at most `maxRounds` (template 3, kit 4, scratch 4).

**Tests:** `test/cyrus-meshgen.test.ts` (29, pure: specs, Python/TS consistency, cost, router, budgets, scan, glb, checks, manifest,
submit/worker on the in-memory queue with a fake runner, node-2 runner against a fake transport, contract).
`test/cyrus-meshgen-blender.test.ts` (3, REAL, skipped unless on node-2 with `CYRUS_MESHGEN_REAL=1`; run with
`devhost run -- env CYRUS_MESHGEN_REAL=1 npx tsx --test test/cyrus-meshgen-blender.test.ts`, NOT `--lock`: each Blender run takes the
lock itself). Real flights: `devhost run -- npx tsx scripts/cyrus/meshgen-flights.ts .meshgen-flights` then `devhost pull`.

- RAN REAL on node-2 2026-10-10 (raw `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-research/meshgen-flights-2026-10-10.json`, renders + glbs
  `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-research/blender-poc/meshgen/`): selftest 16/16 variant cases manifold per shell, 4/4 bad enums raise; 10
  flights through route -> submit -> worker -> sandbox: 9 accepted (rifle x2, crate x2, sword x2, kit terminal, decimation crate
  2,520 -> 1,158 tris under a 1,200 budget, scratch lantern), the hostile script rejected by the in-sandbox guard with the TS scan
  bypassed. 524-2,544 tris, 0 non-manifold edges, Khronos glTF validator 0 errors / 0 warnings on all 9 glbs. Sandbox wall 19-32 s per
  job, of which Cycles rendering is 16-28 s and geometry under 0.05 s; lock wait 2-4 ms (idle host). The rifle AK spec reproduces the
  PoC's 1,452 triangles exactly.
- NOT RUN: any model call (specs/scripts are hand-written fixtures; token figures are estimates), a vision "look" step, LODs, normal
  bakes, boolean union, in-engine load (FiveM/UE/three.js), the catalog integration, a GPU or isolated (microVM) worker, a kernel-escape
  test, the ssh transport from the primary (the flights used the local transport on node-2; the ssh path is unit-tested only).
EOF

# O: Cyrus AI mesh (meshgen) as a service (2026-10-10)

Branch `feature/cyrus-r18-meshgen` (worktree `/tank/dev-worktrees/cyrus-r18`). Flags OFF, not wired into the build service, no migration. Docs: `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` "Cyrus AI mesh (meshgen)". Owner items: OWNER-ACTIONS.md "AI mesh / meshgen service".

## What was built
- `lib/cyrus/meshgen/`: Zod specs (rifle, crate, sword templates; hard-surface kit; scratch submission; job request with budget, estimate, usage), template registry with model-facing spec cards, deterministic router over the cost ladder (0 catalog stub, 1 template, 2 kit, 3 scratch), token/cost estimator (prices are owner settings; none configured = tokens only), budget resolution from a new optional `AssetProfile.meshBudget`, TS GLB parser, post-processing checks, static scan for scripts, manifest + per-job record, node-2 runner, worker loop, model-facing tool contract (types only).
- `blender/`: harness, geometry kit, rifle template + parts (ported from PoC K), NEW crate and sword templates, NEW 10-shape parts kit (rung 2), AST guard for rung 3, `sbx-meshgen.sh` (PoC sandbox plus tmpfs work dir, file-size limit, regular-files-only copy back).
- Small additive changes outside meshgen: `AssetProfile.meshBudget?` (+ validator), `JobQueue.claim({types?})`.

## Ran (real, node-2, 2026-10-10)
Raw: `meshgen-flights-2026-10-10.json`; renders/glbs: `blender-poc/meshgen/`.

| Flight | Rung | Verdict | Tris | Sandbox wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| rifle_ak (PoC spec) | template | accepted | 1,452 (same as PoC) | 26.4 s |
| rifle_drum_lmg | template | accepted | 2,128 | 25.8 s |
| crate_scifi | template | accepted | 2,544 | 27.4 s |
| crate_wooden | template | accepted | 2,376 | 29.2 s |
| sword_knight | template | accepted | 1,330 | 19.6 s |
| sword_katana_glow | template | accepted | 930 | 19.0 s |
| kit_terminal | kit | accepted | 524 | 24.0 s |
| crate_decimate (1,200 budget) | template | accepted, decimated 2,520 -> 1,158 | 1,158 | 31.7 s |
| scratch_lantern | scratch | accepted | 1,368 | 27.1 s |
| scratch_escape (TS scan bypassed) | scratch | rejected by in-sandbox guard (9 issues) | - | 2.7 s |

- Selftest: 16 variant cases (every enum value of every template + kit) build with 0 non-manifold edges; 4 bad-enum cases raise errors naming the allowed values. Khronos glTF validator: 0 errors, 0 warnings on all 9 glbs.
- Time: Cycles rendering is 16-28 s of each run; geometry under 0.05 s. Blender tarball sha256 re-checked: matches the published file.
- Tests: `cyrus-meshgen.test.ts` 29/29, `cyrus-meshgen-blender.test.ts` 3/3 (real), full Cyrus suite + tsc (numbers in the docs section).

My judgement from the renders (not a blind rating): crate_scifi 7.5, lantern (scratch) 7, katana 7, knight sword 6.5, terminal (kit) 6.5, wooden crate 6, drum rifle 5 (the drum magazine reads as a wheel). The decimated crate looks the same as the full one at 46% of the triangles.

## Not run
- Any model call. Every spec and script is a hand-written fixture; token figures are estimates (template and scratch fit the PoC's measured ranges; kit is an assumption).
- Vision "look" step, LODs, normal/AO bakes, boolean union (meshes are closed shells that overlap), UV overlap check, in-engine load (FiveM, UE, three.js).
- Catalog rung against the real catalog (fake matcher only), build-service wiring, plan gate.
- ssh transport from the primary (flights used the local transport on node-2; ssh is unit-tested with a fake).
- Kernel-escape test of the sandbox; isolated (microVM/gVisor) worker; GPU worker.

## Decisions made here
- Catalog fit "unknown" never routes to rung 0; threshold 0.75.
- Template choice needs a keyword hit; category alone never selects a template; exclude words win ("revolver" never gets the rifle).
- Characters/creatures/likeness refused on every rung; organic shapes only on rung 3.
- A rejected mesh stores renders but never the glb or manifest. `outputs[0]` is always the record.
- Busy build host = not_run + job failed (resubmit), never a silent wait past the job timeout.
- Manifest `provenance.generator` (proposed in the plan) is not added (the manifest is strict and shared); the generator `ai-mesh` is in the record and the manifest note.

## Next
Paid eval (20+ prompts per rung, real tokens and success rate), vision look step, isolated worker for rung 3, real game budgets, more templates (pistol/shotgun, furniture, axe/hammer), fix the drum magazine variant.

input.message:
Meshgen (Model Studio layer 4) is built as a service on `feature/cyrus-r18-meshgen` in `/tank/dev-worktrees/cyrus-r18` (commits 209f6d3cd1, ec68aa3b9d, 18bf012e95). It is behind `CYRUS_MESHGEN` and `CYRUS_MESHGEN_SCRATCH` (both off), not wired into the build service, no migration.

Code is in `lib/cyrus/meshgen/`:
- a router that picks the cheapest rung (catalog stub, template, parts kit, from-scratch script) and estimates tokens; dollars stay empty until the owner sets prices;
- templates: rifle (ported) plus new crate and sword, and a new 10-shape parts kit;
- a node-2 sandbox runner, a job-queue worker, glb/budget checks, and a glb plus manifest marked `ai-generated-for-user`, source `ai`;
- the tool contract the build service would use (types only).

Real node-2 runs:
- All 16 template/kit variant builds were manifold per shell.
- 9 of 9 flights were accepted, including the kit, the from-scratch lantern and decimation (2,520 to 1,158 triangles). The Khronos validator found 0 errors on every glb.
- A hostile script was rejected inside the sandbox even with the TypeScript scan bypassed.
- Each run took 19-32 s, mostly rendering.

Suites: unit 29/29, real Blender 3/3, tsc clean. After merging r2 the Cyrus suite was 1501/1502; `cyrus-admin` failed in the batch but passes 31/31 alone.

Not run: any model call (specs are my hand-written fixtures, token figures are estimates), LODs, in-engine load, a kernel-escape test, an isolated worker. The rifle's drum magazine looks like a wheel.

Outputs: `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-research/O-meshgen.md`, `meshgen-flights-2026-10-10.json`, `blender-poc/meshgen/`, an OWNER-ACTIONS.md section, and the "Cyrus AI mesh (meshgen)" section in `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`.
